Case studies

Payments
Signup
Flow

Role Senior Content Designer
Scope Onboarding · Verification · FTU · AI assistant · Invoicing
Methods Usability testing · Content audit · Journey mapping · Iteration
Problem

Fewer than 1 in 3 merchants completed Payments setup.

QuickBooks Payments had a strong product but a content problem. Setup completion sat below 30% — not because the flow was too long, but because merchants couldn't see what they'd get at the end. The onboarding was built around compliance logic, not customer goals. Merchants hit jargon-heavy screens, ambiguous choices, and no clear sense of what finishing would make possible.

Research

Merchants didn't know what they were signing up for.

Usability sessions and unmoderated tests revealed a consistent pattern: merchants weren't confused by the steps — they were uncertain about the destination. 6 of 7 participants called Payments their most important feature. Most still couldn't complete setup without help.

A full content audit mapped every screen against what merchants actually needed at that moment. Most were answering questions nobody had asked — and missing the one question everyone had: what will I be able to do when this is done?

"I don't know which one to pick. What if I pick the wrong one and can't change it?" — Merchant, usability session

Iterations

Lead with the outcome. Earn every word after that.

I reframed every setup screen around what merchants would be able to do — not what they needed to provide. I tested multiple content approaches for payment method selection, iterating from feature-led to use-case-led to customer-experience-led framing. For the AI assistant, early versions over-explained. Each iteration cut further — one suggestion, one action, done.

FTU setup checklist — "choose how to get paid"

Payments agent — congrats on first payment request

Intuit Assist — empty state before customer selected

Intuit Assist — populated with customer context

Solution

Content mapped to every stage of the merchant journey.

The final system gave each lifecycle stage a clear content goal and a matched AI message — from first setup through ongoing use. The AI invoice assistant got a full content framework: proactive suggestions grounded in merchant data, adjustable-tone reminders, AI-driven late fee recommendations, and a "good to go" state that confirmed completion without adding noise.

Review and edit invoice reminders — tone selector

Scheduled reminders — preview with merchant controls

Late fee suggestion — AI recommendation with merchant data

Late fees applied — "Good to go"

Impact

Setup completion jumped from under 30% to over 60%.

<30% → 60%+
Payments setup completion rate — before and after
4×
Growth in monthly payment volume during this period (Intuit FY2024)
21%
YoY growth in online services revenue driven by Payments (Intuit FY2024)

Content
Guidance
& AI Strategy

Role Content Strategy Lead
Scope AI voice & tone · Content principles · GenAI team collaboration · Writer training
Audience GenAI engineers · Content designers · PMs · Product designers
Problem

AI was shipping fast. Nobody agreed on how it should sound.

As Intuit's GenAI team built agentic features across QuickBooks, a content gap emerged: there were no shared standards for how AI should speak to customers. Engineers wrote prompt templates without content review. Writers made different calls on the same problems. With 74% of Intuit Assist customers saying AI improved their financial picture, the stakes for getting the content right were only getting higher.

Research

The AI was saying too much — and giving itself too much credit.

I embedded with the GenAI team to audit AI-generated content across QuickBooks: agentic suggestions, proactive tips, completion messages, and invoice reminders generated at scale. Two patterns stood out. Agents were front-loading information customers didn't need yet — creating cognitive load instead of reducing it. And the language centered the AI rather than the customer: "I drafted $1,000 worth of invoices for you to review" instead of "$1,000 worth of invoices are ready for your review."

I also reviewed the Python prompt codebase to understand where content decisions were baked into engineering — and where a content framework could intercept them.

Collaboration

Writing the rules together — with engineers in the room.

I worked directly with the GenAI engineering and product team to develop content principles that would work inside the prompt architecture — practical enough to actually change how the team wrote. We landed on three core principles: stay focused on what the customer gets done, not what the AI did; use first person only when it helps the customer feel in control; and surface one relevant thing at a time. I then rewrote prompt templates for the invoice reminder system using these principles.

Solution

A content framework the whole team could ship with.

The final framework gave the GenAI team a shared standard for every AI content moment: welcome messages, proactive suggestions, confirmations, error recovery, and disclosures. Each pattern included the principle, the reasoning, and a real before/after from product copy — so engineers and PMs could apply it without a content designer in every room.

Core principles — agents maintain first-person perspective

Do/don't examples — "Accounting done" vs "Accounting done by AI"

The best guide doesn't steal the spotlight. They help you get where you're going — then step aside.

Impact

Consistent AI content. Faster decisions. Less rework after launch.

Writers and PMs stopped debating the same questions and started shipping more confidently. AI features launched with stronger content from day one because the standards existed before the work started — not after. The prompt templates we rewrote together are still running in production, generating customer-facing reminders at scale.

5 days
Faster payment collection with Intuit Payments Agent (Intuit, 2024)
74%
Of Intuit Assist customers say AI gives them a better financial picture (Intuit, 2024)
6 hrs
Saved per month by customers using Intuit AI (Intuit, 2025)
And one more thing

I also trained product designers to catch content mistakes the AI makes.

Guidance only works if people can use it. I created training materials for product designers — visual, concrete, grounded in real product copy — covering the principles most likely to get missed when AI is generating at scale.
